say: Today we're going to work through a hotel coordinator's inbox, not watch a collection of disconnected Copilot tricks. You'll use the practice emails to understand a situation, choose what needs attention, and prepare something useful to do next.
The screens give you a route to follow, but your own response is the material we'll discuss. Finishing quickly matters less than being able to explain why a priority or reply makes sense.
welcome.ask: Which part of a busy inbox usually costs you more effort: understanding, deciding, or replying?
welcome.watch: Let the opening scene settle; distinguish the animated walkthrough from the learner's live Outlook window.

say: Put yourself in the coordinator's seat on this fictional Friday morning: fifteen messages have arrived, and several people need a decision rather than another acknowledgement. Guest concerns and conference preparation are competing for the same attention.

Read the situation as a coordination problem, not simply a pile of emails to clear. Our task is to notice consequences, dependencies, and deadlines without assuming that the loudest message is automatically the most important.
role.ask: What could go wrong if the coordinator answered these messages only in the order they arrived?
role.watch: Point to the competing alerts as they appear; keep discussion within the fictional hotel scenario.

say: Follow the route across the screen: we first understand the messages, then judge priorities, then draft replies, and finally organise the work with other people. Those moves connect because a weak understanding at the start can produce a confident but inappropriate response later.
Most of your hands-on work today is in Outlook and Copilot Chat. The Teams segment at the end is my demonstration of the same reasoning applied to a channel conversation.
plan.ask: Where in this route would you check that a suggested action is actually supported by a message?
plan.watch: Trace the five nodes in order; clarify that learners do not need to set up Teams.

say: Before we begin, check your work account, the Outlook environment shown for this exercise, and your access to Copilot. We'll also need the practice messages, which the next screens help you prepare.

If one of these isn't available, tell me now rather than spending the exercise searching for a missing button. You can still follow the decisions with the demonstration while we resolve access or find the appropriate route for your environment.
needs.ask: Which of the four preparation items still needs checking on your device?
needs.watch: Check actual access rather than treating the animated ticks as confirmation; identify anyone following the demo instead.

say: Enter the address you're using for the practice exercise and download the email ZIP from this page. That gives you the fictional messages we'll all use, rather than asking you to expose your normal inbox.

Notice the option to include full-thread replies, because it affects how many files you'll import later. If you already received the complete practice set before class, use the skip link and meet us at the Outlook tour instead.
get.ask: Are you downloading a new practice set, or do you already have the tagged messages in Outlook?
get.watch: Avoid projecting anyone's address; confirm the download completed and note whether full-thread replies were included.

say: This roadmap separates getting a ZIP onto your computer from putting its messages into Outlook. We'll locate the download, extract it, open the import route, select the extracted folder, choose a destination, and check the result.
Keep the overview in mind, but don't try to memorise every click at once. Each following screen covers one part, and a mismatch is easier to diagnose when we know which part we're on.
road.ask: Which stage changes the downloaded files into messages you can practise with in Outlook?
road.watch: Walk through the roadmap once; keep learners at the same setup stage before advancing.

say: The subject tag is our way to distinguish workshop material from your everyday messages. Look for the square-bracketed Copilot Learning text at the beginning of a practice email's subject.

That gives you a recognisable search term when we check the import, and a way to find the training messages again for cleanup. Use both the tag and the practice folder to stay focused on this exercise rather than accidentally bringing normal correspondence into the discussion.
tag.ask: What exact subject text will you search for when checking the imported practice messages?
tag.watch: Point to the brackets and wording; ensure learners recognise the tag without selecting real messages.

say: Find the ZIP you just downloaded using your browser's download list or the Downloads folder. We're locating a file at this point, not opening Outlook or starting the import yet.

Check that you're looking at the workshop download rather than an older file with a similar name. Knowing where it landed now prevents confusion when the later folder picker asks for the extracted emails instead of the original ZIP.
download.ask: Can you identify the workshop ZIP and the folder where your browser saved it?
download.watch: Pause for learners to locate the file; avoid advancing while anyone is still searching the browser download panel.

say: On the Windows route shown here, right-click the downloaded ZIP and choose Extract All. The purpose is to unpack the email files so that you can select their containing folder for the import.

Don't rename individual messages or move them around while we do this. If you're following on a Mac, the lesson shows a different extraction action; we'll check your resulting folder rather than expecting your menu to match the Windows illustration.
extract1.ask: Are you extracting the ZIP, or only viewing the files inside the compressed download?
extract1.watch: Wait for the extraction dialog; help distinguish a compressed-folder view from an extracted folder.

say: Confirm the extraction and let the resulting folder open. Find the hotel-practice-emails folder and notice where it now lives, because that location is what we'll use in the Outlook picker.

The important result is a folder containing the individual email files, not just another view of the ZIP. Take a moment to check the contents before switching apps, so we don't have to retrace this step during the import.
extract2.ask: Where is your extracted hotel-practice-emails folder, and can you see the email files inside it?
extract2.watch: Check one learner's folder structure with permission; watch for an extra nested folder before the files.

say: Open the Outlook app we're using for the demonstrated import route and check that you're signed into the intended work account. Keep the extracted folder available so you can return to it if needed.

Your screen may not look exactly like the illustration, particularly if you're using a different Outlook environment. Let me know before searching through unrelated menus; the goal is to put the training messages in the right place, not to force a mismatched interface to behave like this one.
openol.ask: Does your Outlook window match the environment shown for the import exercise?
openol.watch: Identify different Outlook versions early; keep learners out of personal accounts.

say: Use the File menu and the Open and export route shown on this screen to reach the import settings. We're moving from the normal mailbox view into the area where the workshop files will be brought in.

Before clicking further, compare your window with the example and locate the import section. If your menus differ, stop at the point of difference so we can help without changing unrelated account or mailbox settings.
filemenu.ask: Can you locate the import settings from the File route on your own screen?
filemenu.watch: Point to Open and export; check that learners reached settings rather than a file-opening dialog.

say: Choose the Email Files option for this exercise, because the extracted practice folder contains individual email files. The other import choice shown is not the route we're following.

Check the label before starting so you don't end up looking for a different kind of file. This is a small setup decision, but choosing the correct input type saves a lot of troubleshooting when the picker opens.
importeml.ask: Which import option matches the individual files in your extracted practice folder?
importeml.watch: Highlight Email Files (.eml), not the Outlook Data File option; pause before Start import.

say: Choose the extracted hotel-practice-emails folder, then confirm the selection in the upload dialog. Don't select the ZIP or a parent folder that doesn't directly contain the messages.

If you included the full-thread replies, this set contains eighteen files: the fifteen practice messages and three additional conversation files. Use that as a setup check, not as a reason to download again if you deliberately chose the smaller set.
upload.ask: Does your selected folder contain the practice email files, and does its count match your download choice?
upload.watch: Check the chosen path and file count before confirmation; distinguish Upload here from the earlier local download.

say: Now choose where these practice messages belong in Outlook, separate from the folder you selected on your computer. Use LEARN-COPILOT as the destination folder for the exercise, creating it only if you don't already have it.

This separation makes the later reading and checking much easier. Before you confirm the import, make sure the selected destination is the practice folder rather than your main inbox or an unrelated folder.
destination.ask: Are you creating LEARN-COPILOT for the first time, or selecting an existing practice folder?
destination.watch: Distinguish the Outlook destination from the extracted source folder; avoid creating duplicate practice folders.

say: Open the practice folder and look for the tagged subjects to confirm that the import produced usable messages. Check the training set itself rather than assuming the completed import dialog tells us everything we need.

The extra full-thread replies already contain their conversations, so don't mistake them for unexpected duplicates of unrelated mail. Once you can open a practice message and recognise its subject tag, we have the material for the hands-on exercises.
check.ask: Can you open a tagged practice message in LEARN-COPILOT and identify whether full-thread replies are present?
check.watch: Verify folder contents and one opened message; compare counts only against the learner's chosen download set.

say: If something doesn't look right, start by checking the extracted source folder, the selected import type, and the Outlook destination. Those checks tell us whether the problem is finding the files, importing them, or looking in the wrong place afterwards.
Show me the stage where your screen diverges rather than starting the whole process again immediately. Repeating an import before checking the destination can make the practice set harder to inspect.
stuck.ask: At which stage did your result first differ: extraction, source selection, or destination checking?
stuck.watch: Troubleshoot one stage at a time; do not recommend repeat imports until the selected destination has been checked.

say: We've reached the first pause: the training messages should now be available in the practice folder. The work so far was setup, and we can leave the import route behind.

Take a breath and check whether you can follow the next exercise in your own mailbox or need to work from my demonstration. There's no new task on this checkpoint; it's a chance to make sure everyone is ready to start interpreting the messages.
cp1.ask: Who can open the practice messages now, and who still needs help before the Outlook tour?
cp1.watch: Resolve remaining setup issues or arrange demo-following; don't turn the checkpoint into another import exercise.

say: Notice the three areas we'll use repeatedly: the folder list, the message list, and the reading pane. Choosing the practice folder gives you the relevant set, while choosing a message shows the actual evidence.

Keep that relationship in mind when we later inspect a Copilot answer. A summary or recommendation needs to lead us back to a specific message, and these are the places you'll use to find and read it.
tour.ask: Where would you go to check the original email behind a suggested action?
tour.watch: Point to each pane in sequence; confirm LEARN-COPILOT is selected before learners explore.

say: Select a practice email and read it in the pane on the right before asking Copilot anything. Look beyond the subject to what the sender needs, what has already happened, and whether the message gives a time for your response.

The unread styling helps you navigate, but it doesn't tell you how urgent the situation is. Understanding the request first gives you a reference point for judging the summary and reply we'll generate later.
read.ask: What is the sender asking the coordinator to do, rather than merely know?
read.watch: Allow silent reading time; keep attention on the message body instead of treating bold subjects as priorities.

say: Use these three questions to turn a message into a priority decision: what is the impact, when does that impact matter, and what deadline is actually stated? A guest problem and a routine administration request can both be politely worded while carrying very different consequences.
Separate a deadline in the email from a time you think would be sensible. That distinction matters when we ask Copilot to organise the inbox and then inspect its reasoning.
questions.ask: For the message you opened, what deadline is explicit and what timing would require your own judgement?
questions.watch: Ask learners to point to supporting wording; challenge urgency inferred only from tone or subject.

say: Look across all fifteen messages and try grouping them before checking a generated priority list. Guest safety and immediate operational disruption deserve a different discussion from work that can wait.

The sample ordering is a way to compare reasoning, not a compulsory ranking to reproduce. If your ordering differs, explain the consequence or deadline that led you there, then use the original message to see whether that explanation holds up.
sort.ask: Which two messages would you place first, and what evidence makes them more urgent than the others?
sort.watch: Invite one defensible alternative ordering; distinguish disagreement about judgement from incorrect reading of facts.

say: Find the Copilot entry point in the Outlook window so you know where the later exercises begin. The walkthrough also points out a thread-summary route, which is useful to recognise when opening a longer conversation.
We aren't asking for an answer on this screen yet. Make sure you know which email or thread is selected, because the next task needs the right context rather than simply the right-looking icon.
cop.ask: Which message or thread is selected when you open the Copilot entry point on your screen?
cop.watch: Locate the actual control in the learner's environment; avoid clicking into an unrelated message.

say: For the inbox-wide exercise, open the work chat route shown in the lesson and check the context control in your own interface. The screen illustrates different labels you might encounter, so we'll compare what you actually see rather than search for one exact arrangement.

Our question concerns the workshop emails, not a general answer about hotel coordination. If the response doesn't connect to those messages, treat that as a context problem to investigate before judging the priority list.
chat.ask: What on your screen indicates you're using the intended work context for today's practice emails?
chat.watch: Check the displayed Work or Work IQ control without assuming every interface matches; don't project normal mailbox content.

say: Copy the first prompt and ask which of today's emails need a response or action, including the subject, request, deadline, and recommended next step. Notice that we're asking for the basis of the priority, not just a numbered list.
Keep your attention on the practice set when the answer comes back. If it brings in other correspondence or invents a missing deadline, we need to correct the scope before using the recommendation.
t1do.ask: Which requested field will make this priority list easiest to verify against your practice emails?
t1do.watch: Confirm the copied prompt and practice scope; wait for real learner responses before moving to the check screen.

say: Read your own priority answer beside the checking questions, using the illustrated result only as an example of structure. Trace each listed item to an actual practice message and compare the explanation with its impact and deadline.

A missing message can matter just as much as an invented one, so inspect the coverage too. Where you disagree with the order, decide whether the facts were read incorrectly or whether your judgement about the consequences is different.
t1ok.ask: Which recommendation in your real answer would you keep or change, and which email supports your decision?
t1ok.watch: Do not present the sample ranking as the learner's result; check one citation, one deadline, and any omitted item.

say: Open the prepared ballroom conversation and use the long-thread prompt to separate the situation, confirmed facts, decisions, unresolved issues, and actions. These categories stop a suggestion buried in the thread from becoming a decision in the summary.

The ending asks for the most urgent next action, which should follow from the conversation rather than from a guess. If you use the dependency follow-up, check whether each update time is actually mentioned.
t2do.ask: What would you need to see in the thread before calling a backup-room suggestion a confirmed decision?
t2do.watch: Ensure the full prepared conversation is selected, not an isolated reply; keep the five requested categories visible.

say: Check the summary you received against the full ballroom thread, especially where it separates something proposed from something decided. The illustration highlights cooling, the backup room, and several update times, but it isn't proof of what your answer contains.

A concise summary is useful only if it preserves the uncomfortable parts of the situation. Look for unresolved capacity or timing issues and confirm that the final urgent action hasn't silently assumed a repair or approval.
t2ok.ask: Where does your summary preserve an unresolved issue instead of turning it into a confirmed solution?
t2ok.watch: Trace one time and one decision to the original thread; do not treat the sample backup recommendation as guaranteed.

say: We've practised two different ways of understanding work: looking across the inbox and reading one conversation deeply. The common skill is checking what the messages support before deciding what matters.

Hold onto one example where you corrected or questioned the answer, because that judgement carries into drafting replies. There's nothing new to submit here; we're pausing before changing from interpretation to communication.
cp2.ask: Which distinction helped you most: urgent versus routine, or confirmed versus unresolved?
cp2.watch: Take one short reflection; make sure learners have completed their checks before moving to reply drafting.

say: Open the guest concern and ask for a caring, professional reply that acknowledges the problem and states the next step. The prompt deliberately blocks guarantees about rooms, compensation, and benefits that aren't confirmed in the message.

That boundary doesn't prevent warmth; it prevents warmth from turning into an unsupported commitment. Let Copilot draft the wording, then we'll check whether it shows ownership while staying honest about what the coordinator knows.
t3do.ask: How could the reply show care without promising that a replacement room is already available?
t3do.watch: Use Draft with Copilot on the fictional guest email; keep the learner in draft mode and away from Send.

say: Read the draft you actually received, not just the example on the screen, as if you were the guest who reported the concern. Check that it understands the request, shows responsibility, and makes the next step clear.

Then inspect every sentence that sounds like a promise, including any claim that a team is already on its way. A caring tone and a short word count don't make an unsupported action true, so revise the wording before considering it usable.
t3ok.ask: Which sentence in your draft needs evidence before you could safely send it?
t3ok.watch: Check names and booking details against the fictional email; flag unsupported dispatch, availability, or compensation wording.

say: Now open the vendor message about the missing microphones and request a concise operational reply. We need the impact, the requested action, the response time, a temporary option, and an escalation contact rather than a vague request to help.

Keep the distinction between asking for a solution and saying it has been agreed. The draft should make the vendor's next response easier while keeping the rehearsal and conference needs connected to the evidence.
t4do.ask: What does the vendor need to confirm so that the coordinator can make a practical next decision?
t4do.watch: Use the microphone vendor practice email; check that the generated request doesn't invent an agreed delivery.

say: Inspect your vendor draft against the five requirements shown, then trace any time or equipment detail back to the email. The illustrated reply is a comparison aid, not a message you should automatically copy.

Look especially at whether a temporary option is requested or accidentally presented as already approved. A good operational reply tells the vendor what is needed and by when, while leaving room for a truthful confirmation or an escalation.
t4ok.ask: Does your draft distinguish the requested temporary solution from something the vendor has already confirmed?
t4ok.watch: Check the rehearsal, delivery, and response times in the real draft; don't endorse the sample timings without tracing them.

say: You've now worked on two different tones: care for a guest and precision with a vendor. Both still depend on the same boundary between a supported next step and a promise we can't justify.

Take this pause to save or retain your reviewed drafts without sending practice correspondence. Next we'll look beyond individual replies and organise the work those messages create across the rest of the day.
cp3.ask: What changed between your guest and vendor replies, and what review habit stayed the same?
cp3.watch: Confirm drafts remain unsent; invite a brief comparison of tone rather than another rewrite.

say: Use the day-planning prompt to turn the priority messages into grouped actions: immediate work, work before noon, afternoon tasks, delegation or escalation, and updates to monitor. Ask for a reason and any deadline so the plan can be challenged.

Grouping isn't the same as solving the problems. Read each action as a proposal for managing attention, and check whether it assigns work sensibly without handing off a decision that remains the coordinator's responsibility.
t5do.ask: Which item should be monitored for an update rather than treated as a completed action?
t5do.watch: Keep the plan tied to the practice priorities; watch for invented deadlines or unsupported completed actions.

say: Look at the plan you received and test it against the time available and the actual email requests. The lanes on the slide illustrate a possible structure, but your answer needs its own review.

Check whether an item appears in more than one group for a sensible reason, such as escalation followed by monitoring. Most importantly, make sure delegation doesn't erase your responsibility to confirm a decision or provide the next update.
t5ok.ask: Which action in your real plan would you keep ownership of even if another team does the work?
t5ok.watch: Review one delegated item and its follow-up; don't describe the sample plan as evidence that issues are resolved.

say: Use the conference-related conversation to request a twenty-five-minute agenda covering cooling, catering, microphones, communications, and decisions. Each item needs a purpose as well as a time allocation.

The final five minutes are reserved for decisions, owners, and deadlines, so the meeting doesn't end with everyone merely informed. When the answer arrives, we'll test both the arithmetic and whether the agenda can lead to useful outcomes without assuming approvals that haven't happened.
t6do.ask: What should the team leave with after the final five minutes of this agenda?
t6do.watch: Use the conference context despite any legacy summary-style mock labels; check the actual prompt requests an agenda.

say: Add up the allocations in your actual agenda and check that the total is twenty-five minutes, with the last five protected for decisions. The sample split on screen is only one possible allocation.

Read the purpose beside each topic and ask whether it moves the meeting toward a choice, confirmation, or next action. A topic list that uses the right minutes can still be weak if it never says what the participants need to resolve.
t6ok.ask: Which agenda item in your answer needs a clearer decision purpose, even if its time allocation is correct?
t6ok.watch: Calculate the learner's total aloud; inspect the final five-minute purpose rather than relying on the illustrated time bar.

say: For this part, watch my demonstration rather than setting up your own channel. The fictional posts show several teams discussing cooling, food, equipment, and what to tell the organiser.

Notice that updates, questions, and possible decisions are mixed together in a conversation that keeps moving. Before we ask for a catch-up, pick out one unanswered question so we can later judge whether the summary preserves it.
teams1.ask: Which question in the displayed channel still needs a response or decision?
teams1.watch: Let each fictional post appear; remind learners this is trainer-led and not a requirement to create a Teams channel.

say: I'll use the catch-up prompt to request important updates, decisions, unresolved questions, and actions with references to the relevant posts. It's the same separation we used with the long email thread, now applied to a channel.

Compare the live demonstration response with the messages rather than expecting the illustration to appear word for word. If a question has become a decision in the summary, we need to correct that before anyone relies on it.
teams2.ask: Does the demonstrated response keep the backup-room and approval questions open where the messages leave them open?
teams2.watch: Verify references against the displayed channel; describe the example card as illustrative if no live demo response is available.

say: The planning and collaboration moves are now complete: you've proposed a day plan, checked an agenda, and seen a channel catch-up. None of those outputs means the underlying hotel issues have been resolved.

The value is a clearer view of what to do, who needs to decide, and what still needs an update. We'll pause here before the short challenge so you can separate a useful plan from a claim of completed work.
cp4.ask: Which output clarified the next action most for you: the day plan, agenda, or channel catch-up?
cp4.watch: Keep the checkpoint reflective; avoid implying the simulated conference is now operationally ready.

say: Bring the four habits together: use the fictional training material, inspect every answer, reject invented commitments, and keep the final decision with a person. These aren't extra checks after the work; they belong inside every exercise we've done.

Think back to a draft or summary that sounded convincing before you traced it to the source. That's exactly where a deliberate pause helps protect both the guest experience and the coordinator's responsibility.
safe.ask: Which unsupported claim would be most damaging in this scenario: availability, a deadline, or a confirmed action?
safe.watch: Connect each habit to a real learner review example; don't introduce normal guest emails for comparison.

say: Choose one practice email for the four-minute challenge and work through the whole loop: understand it, decide its priority, draft a response, then review and edit. Use the prompt pack if you need it rather than spending the time inventing a new prompt.
The aim isn't a perfect answer or a sent message. Be ready to explain one judgement you made and one sentence you checked or changed before you would use the response.
challenge.ask: What did you change after reviewing your challenge draft, and why?
challenge.watch: Run a real four-minute timer; leave time for review and keep all practice replies unsent.

say: Look back at the route from the busy inbox to clearer action: we read, prioritised, responded, planned, and prepared to collaborate. The same fictional messages became different outputs because we changed the question and the purpose.

The important result isn't reproducing the illustrated answers. It's being able to connect a recommendation to evidence, notice uncertainty, and communicate a next step with the judgement and care the coordinator's role requires.
recap.ask: Which move would you repeat first on a busy morning, and what would you check before using its output?
recap.watch: Trace the recap stages to completed exercises; invite one concrete transfer idea without opening real mailbox content.

say: Keep the prompt pack as a practical reminder of the questions we've practised, including the follow-ups for priorities and dependencies. You can copy an individual prompt or download the set for later reference.

Before reusing one, adapt its scope and purpose to the work in front of you and retain the review boundaries. A saved prompt is a starting point for a task, not permission to accept whatever answer it produces.
pack.ask: Which prompt or follow-up would you save for your next coordination task?
pack.watch: Show copy and download separately; check learners retain the prompt pack rather than the illustrative answers.

say: You've practised finding actions, reading conversations, writing different kinds of replies, organising a day, and preparing people to work together. Those skills belong together because the coordinator has to connect information with responsible action.

Carry three habits with you: check the source, keep unsupported promises out, and make your own judgement before using the output. Choose one small workflow to practise next rather than trying to change your whole working day at once.
learned.ask: What is one task you'll practise next, and what personal review check will you pair with it?
learned.watch: Close with a specific learner commitment; remind the group to identify and clean up tagged practice material when appropriate.
